title: Structured Prompts to Complete a Task
summary: Students learn the Goal-Context-Format prompt structure, use it to complete a defined task on a teacher-operated tool, judge whether the task was completed, and make one adjustment to complete it more fully.
objectives: Use a structured prompt to complete a defined task with an AI tool.
Describe the input structure used and whether the task was completed.
Adjust the prompt once to complete the task more fully.

sections.heading: Structured Prompts to Complete a Task
body: Ask an AI tool a vague question and you get a vague answer. Learn to structure your prompt and you can actually get a task done. Today you learn the trick: **Goal, Context, Format**.

sections.heading: I can…
items: I can write a structured prompt with a clear goal, context and format.
I can say whether the task was completed and why.
I can improve my prompt once to complete the task more fully.

terms.definition: The instruction you give an AI tool.
A prompt with a clear goal, context and format.
What you want the tool to do.
The details the tool needs to do it.
How you want the answer to look.

sections.heading: Goal, Context, Format
body: A vague prompt like 'tell me about the desert' leaves the tool guessing. A [[structured prompt]] tells it exactly what to do.
**Goal**: what you want. **Context**: the details it needs. **Format**: how the answer should look. Together they make the task far more likely to be completed.

sections.heading: Check, then improve
body: Once you get an output, compare it to the task. Did it do everything you asked? If not, change one thing in your prompt and try again.
Two safety rules: never put personal data in a prompt, and always verify the answer - a confident output can still be wrong.

sections.label: Let's try it - hands-on
sections.heading: Let's try it - hands-on
body: Write a structured prompt for a real task, judge whether it completed the task, and improve it once.
items: Underline what 'complete' means for your task.
Write your prompt with Goal, Context and Format.
Watch the teacher run it on the approved tool.
Judge whether the task was completed.
Adjust your prompt once and verify the output.

sections.heading: Think about it
items: Which part of the structure helped most?
How did you know the task was or was not complete?

sections.heading: My reflection
items: Write the one adjustment that improved your result.
Write one safety rule you used today.

worksheet.title: Week 3 - Core - Worksheet | Structured Prompts to Complete a Task

questions.lookFor: All three parts present and specific: Goal (what to do), Context (details the tool needs), Format (how the answer should look). Emerging (expected) is a prompt with a clear goal, context and format; two of the three parts is approaching; a vague or unstructured prompt is not yet. Structure beats length - a short, clear frame can be stronger than a long rambling one. No personal or identifying data in the context.

questions.stem:
Task complete? ___ because ___
My one adjustment: ___
questions.lookFor: Look for judgement against the task, not just 'it looks good' - for example 'Not fully - it gave four bullets but I asked for three, and one was off-topic.' The adjustment should be one clear change that improves completion, such as adding 'Give exactly three bullet points, each under 12 words.' Emerging (expected): judges completion accurately against the task and makes one adjustment that improves completion.

This is the lesson's main evidence. The log should show a structured prompt, a summary of the output, a 'task complete?' judgement made against the task, and one adjustment that improved completion. Accept a partly completed task if the judgement and adjustment are honest and specific.

questions.stem: What are the three parts of a structured prompt, and which helped you most today?
questions.lookFor: Goal (what to do), Context (details the tool needs), Format (how the answer should look). All three must be present, in the student's own wording and in any order or layout. The second half is a personal judgement - accept any one of the three parts as long as a reason is given.

questions.stem: Add an 'Audience' part to your prompt and describe how it changed the output.
questions.lookFor: Stretch task: the student adds a fourth element (Audience) and shows how it improved the output. Look for a named audience in the prompt and a described change in the output that can be traced to it.
